answer.summary: The minimum total sample size required for development of a binary clinical prediction model meeting Riley precision criteria (pmsampsize 1.1.3) is **662 participants**, yielding approximately 115 events. This sample size satisfies three criteria: (1) small overfitting with shrinkage ≥ 0.9 (achieved 0.9052), (2) small absolute difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared ≤ 0.05 (binding constraint at n=662), and (3) precise estimation of average outcome risk within ±0.05 margin of error (achieved ±0.02888 at n=662). The anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared of 0.288 converts to Nagelkerke R-squared of 0.1682, reflecting modest model discrimination.
answer.method: Riley et al. (2018, 2020) precision-based sample size calculation for binary prediction model development as implemented in pmsampsize version 1.1.3. The package computes the minimum sample size meeting three criteria: (1) overfitting control via expected shrinkage of predictor effects (target ≥0.9), (2) precision of Nagelkerke R-squared estimate (maximum acceptable difference between apparent and adjusted values: 0.05), and (3) precision of average outcome risk on the probability scale (target margin of error ±0.05). The sample size returned is the maximum across the three criteria-specific requirements. Cox-Snell R-squared input (0.288) is converted internally to Nagelkerke R-squared using R_N = R_CS / (2 - R_CS) for binary outcomes. Shrinkage adjustment uses the multiplicative factor λ = 0.90 as specified.
assumptions: Riley et al. (2018, 2020) precision criteria applied for binary logistic prediction model development
Cox-Snell R-squared 0.288 is the anticipated adjusted R-squared (not apparent) from previous studies or conservative projection
Outcome prevalence 0.174 is stable and representative of the target development population
Shrinkage factor λ = 0.90 specified, indicating acceptable tolerance for 10% shrinkage of predictor effects
Precision criterion uses 95% confidence level with maximum acceptable |apparent - adjusted| Nagelkerke R² difference of 0.05 (package default)
Average outcome-risk margin of error target 0.05 is specified on the absolute probability scale
Binary logistic outcome with 24 candidate predictor parameters (excluding intercept)
No attrition or loss-to-follow-up adjustment applied; sample size is for analyzable participants
Events-per-variable rules NOT applied per user specification; sample size determined entirely by Riley precision criteria
limitations: Cox-Snell R-squared value 0.288 is an anticipation; actual model performance depends on data quality, effect sizes, and predictor selection
Margin of error 0.05 for average outcome risk assumes simple prevalence estimation; prediction model recalibration and discriminative ability precision may require different sample sizes
Sample size does not account for missing data, dropout, or protocol violations; this is the theoretical minimum for complete-case analysis
pmsampsize calculates for a single fixed outcome prevalence; heterogeneous populations may require stratified analysis or larger samples
Conversion from Cox-Snell to Nagelkerke R-squared (0.288 → 0.1682) indicates modest discriminative ability; independent external validation strongly recommended before clinical deployment
Package assumes logistic regression framework; other model types (e.g., tree-based, ensemble methods) may have different precision properties

# Install and load pmsampsize 1.1.3 for Riley criteria binary prediction model sample size
# Ensure we have the correct package version
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize")
}

library(pmsampsize)
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Define parameters for binary prediction model
# Parameters: 24 candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
# Prevalence: 0.174
# Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared: 0.288
# Shrinkage: 0.90
# Precision criterion: max absolute (apparent - adjusted) R-squared = 0.05 on Nagelkerke scale
# Confidence: 95% (default)
# Outcome precision: margin of error 0.05 on risk scale

# Call pmsampsize for binary outcome with Riley criteria
ssize <- pmsampsize(
  type = "binary",
  rsquared = 0.288,  # Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = 24,    # Number of candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
  prevalence = 0.174, # Outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.90,   # Shrinkage factor
  margin = 0.05       # Margin of error for average outcome-risk (absolute)
)

# Display results
print(ssize)

# Extract key values
sample_size_total <- ssize$sample_size
print(paste("Minimum total sample size:", sample_size_total))

# Verify key parameters used
print(paste("Number of parameters:", ssize$parameters))
print(paste("Prevalence:", ssize$prevalence))
print(paste("Anticipated Cox-Snell R-squared:", ssize$rsquared))
print(paste("Shrinkage factor:", ssize$shrinkage))
print(paste("Margin of error:", ssize$margin))

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# Load pmsampsize
library(pmsampsize)

# Call pmsampsize for binary outcome with Riley criteria
# Using csrsquared = 0.288 (anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared)
# parameters = 24 (number of candidate predictors)
# prevalence = 0.174 (outcome prevalence)
# shrinkage = 0.90 (default shrinkage factor)

ssize <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",                # Binary outcome
  csrsquared = 0.288,        # Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = 24,           # Number of candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
  prevalence = 0.174,        # Outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.90           # Shrinkage factor
)

# Display full results
print(ssize)

# Extract key values
cat("\n=== EXTRACTED KEY RESULTS ===\n")
print(paste("Minimum total sample size:", ssize$sample_size))
print(paste("Number of events required:", ssize$events))
print(paste("Number of parameters:", ssize$parameters))
print(paste("Prevalence:", ssize$prevalence))
print(paste("Cox-Snell R-squared:", ssize$csrsquared))
print(paste("Shrinkage factor:", ssize$shrinkage))

# Verify that the sample size meets all three criteria
cat("\n=== CRITERIA VERIFICATION ===\n")
print("Riley criteria for binary outcomes:")
print("1. Small overfitting (shrinkage ≥ 0.9)")
print("2. Small absolute difference (apparent - adjusted Nagelkerke R² ≤ 0.05)")
print("3. Precise estimation of average outcome risk (margin of error ± 0.05)")

# Display the criteria matrix
cat("\nSample size requirements by criterion:\n")
print(ssize$criteria_table)

# Convert Cox-Snell to Nagelkerke for verification
cs_r2 <- ssize$csrsquared
nagelkerke_r2 <- cs_r2 / (2 - cs_r2)
cat(paste("\nCox-Snell R² =", cs_r2, "\n"))
cat(paste("Nagelkerke R² =", round(nagelkerke_r2, 4), "\n"))

# At the returned sample size, verify precision on outcome-risk scale
# Standard error of predicted probability is approximately sqrt(p(1-p)/n) for binary outcome
n_total <- ssize$sample_size
p_prevalence <- ssize$prevalence
se_risk <- sqrt(p_prevalence * (1 - p_prevalence) / n_total)
margin_of_error <- 1.96 * se_risk  # 95% CI

cat(paste("\nAt sample size n =", n_total, ":\n"))
cat(paste("Prevalence p =", p_prevalence, "\n"))
cat(paste("Standard error of p = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) =", round(se_risk, 5), "\n"))
cat(paste("95% margin of error (±1.96 SE) =", round(margin_of_error, 5), "\n"))
cat(paste("Target margin of error = 0.05\n"))

Package default precision criteria used (95% confidence level)
Shrinkage factor of 0.90 applied to adjust for overfitting
Events-per-variable rules NOT applied; sample size determined by precision criteria alone
Cox-Snell R-squared value 0.288 represents anticipated model discrimination after development

Average outcome-risk margin of error 0.05 refers to predictive accuracy on outcome scale

pmsampsize 1.1.3 implements Riley criteria; converts Cox-Snell to Nagelkerke R-squared for binary outcomes using formula R_N = R_CS / (2 - R_CS)
Shrinkage factor (λ = 0.90) moderates optimism adjustment in model performance estimates
Margin of error specification targets absolute precision in predicted risk calibration
Verification: achieved power/precision at returned sample size and preceding integer

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

# Load pmsampsize
library(pmsampsize)

# Call pmsampsize for binary outcome with Riley criteria
# Using csrsquared = 0.288 (anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared)
# parameters = 24 (number of candidate predictors)
# prevalence = 0.174 (outcome prevalence)
# shrinkage = 0.90 (default shrinkage factor)

ssize <- pmsampsize(
  type = "b",                # Binary outcome
  csrsquared = 0.288,        # Anticipated adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  parameters = 24,           # Number of candidate predictors (excluding intercept)
  prevalence = 0.174,        # Outcome prevalence
  shrinkage = 0.90           # Shrinkage factor
)

# Display full results
print(ssize)

# Extract key values
cat("\n=== EXTRACTED KEY RESULTS ===\n")
print(paste("Minimum total sample size:", ssize$sample_size))
print(paste("Number of events required:", ssize$events))
print(paste("Number of parameters:", ssize$parameters))
print(paste("Prevalence:", ssize$prevalence))
print(paste("Cox-Snell R-squared:", ssize$csrsquared))
print(paste("Shrinkage factor:", ssize$shrinkage))

# Verify that the sample size meets all three criteria
cat("\n=== CRITERIA VERIFICATION ===\n")
print("Riley criteria for binary outcomes:")
print("1. Small overfitting (shrinkage ≥ 0.9)")
print("2. Small absolute difference (apparent - adjusted Nagelkerke R² ≤ 0.05)")
print("3. Precise estimation of average outcome risk (margin of error ± 0.05)")

# Display the criteria matrix
cat("\nSample size requirements by criterion:\n")
print(ssize$criteria_table)

# Convert Cox-Snell to Nagelkerke for verification
cs_r2 <- ssize$csrsquared
nagelkerke_r2 <- cs_r2 / (2 - cs_r2)
cat(paste("\nCox-Snell R² =", cs_r2, "\n"))
cat(paste("Nagelkerke R² =", round(nagelkerke_r2, 4), "\n"))

# At the returned sample size, verify precision on outcome-risk scale
# Standard error of predicted probability is approximately sqrt(p(1-p)/n) for binary outcome
n_total <- ssize$sample_size
p_prevalence <- ssize$prevalence
se_risk <- sqrt(p_prevalence * (1 - p_prevalence) / n_total)
margin_of_error <- 1.96 * se_risk  # 95% CI

cat(paste("\nAt sample size n =", n_total, ":\n"))
cat(paste("Prevalence p =", p_prevalence, "\n"))
cat(paste("Standard error of p = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) =", round(se_risk, 5), "\n"))
cat(paste("95% margin of error (±1.96 SE) =", round(margin_of_error, 5), "\n"))
cat(paste("Target margin of error = 0.05\n"))

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the

_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,

          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ A_ u_ t_ h_ o_ r(_ s):

     Collins GS. Minimum sample size required for developing a
     multivariable prediction model: Part I continuous outcomes.
     _Statistics in Medicine_. 2018 (in-press). doi: 10.1002/sim.7993

     Riley RD, Snell KIE, Ensor J, Burke DL, Harrell FE, Jr., Moons KG,
     Collins GS. Minimum sample size required for developing a
     multivariable prediction model: Part II binary and time-to-event

     Cox-Snell R2 from a reported C statistic (AUROC) to inform sample

     outcome. _Statistics in Medicine_. 2020

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

plan.estimand: R-squared test against zero in linear regression with 4 model terms (intercept + 3 predictors)
plan.hypothesis: H0: R² = 0 vs H1: R² > 0 (noncentral F-test)
assumptions: Linear model specification correct
Predictors are fixed (not random)
Errors are normally distributed with constant variance
Multiple correlation ρ = 0.30 holds at population
No multicollinearity issues affecting F-test validity
One-sided test: H1 specifies R² > 0
scientific_notes: Power calculation for F-test of model significance uses noncentral F distribution
Noncentrality parameter λ = n × R² / (1 − R²) derived from effect size f² = R² / (1 − R²)
Numerator df = k = 3 (number of predictors)
Denominator df = n − k − 1 = 80 − 3 − 1 = 76
Critical value from central F(3, 76) at α = 0.05, then compare to noncentral F distribution

answer.summary: For a linear regression model with intercept and 3 predictors tested against R² = 0 (omnibus F-test), with 80 participants, anticipated multiple correlation ρ = 0.30, and significance level α = 0.05 (one-sided), the noncentral F-test power is 0.624.
answer.method: Noncentral F-distribution. The test statistic F = [R²/k] / [(1−R²)/(n−k−1)] follows a central F(k, n−k−1) distribution under H₀. Under H₁, it follows a noncentral F distribution with noncentrality parameter λ = n·R²/(1−R²). Power is computed as P(F > F_crit) where F_crit is the upper α quantile of the central F(k, n−k−1) distribution, evaluated under the noncentral F distribution with the specified λ. Here k=3 predictors, n=80 participants, R²=(0.30)²=0.09, df_num=3, df_den=76, λ=7.912.
assumptions: Linear regression model correctly specified with intercept and 3 fixed predictors
Population multiple correlation coefficient ρ = 0.30
Residuals are normally distributed with homogeneous variance
No multicollinearity interfering with F-test validity
One-sided test: H₀: R² = 0 vs H₁: R² > 0
Significance level α = 0.05 fixed prospectively
limitations: Power estimate depends on the assumed population multiple correlation of 0.30; other effect sizes will yield different power
No allowance made for model misspecification, missing assumptions, or violations of linearity and homogeneity
Design assumes complete data and no attrition
Power reflects the omnibus test of all 3 predictors; does not address planned contrast or individual predictor tests

# Power calculation for R-squared test in linear regression
# H0: R^2 = 0 vs H1: R^2 > 0

# Parameters
n <- 80                          # Sample size
rho <- 0.30                      # Multiple correlation coefficient
k <- 3                           # Number of predictors (excluding intercept)
alpha <- 0.05                    # Significance level

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k                      # Numerator df = number of predictors
df_den <- n - k - 1             # Denominator df = n - k - 1

# Convert multiple correlation to R-squared
R2 <- rho^2

# Noncentrality parameter lambda for F-distribution
# lambda = n * R^2 / (1 - R^2)
lambda <- n * R2 / (1 - R2)

# Critical F-value from central F distribution at alpha = 0.05
critical_F <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

# Power = P(F > critical_F) under noncentral F distribution with noncentrality lambda
# Using pf with ncp parameter
power <- 1 - pf(critical_F, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda)

# Summary output
cat("=== Linear Regression R-squared Power Calculation ===\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "participants\n")
cat("Number of predictors (k):", k, "\n")
cat("Multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("R-squared:", R2, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("\n--- Degrees of Freedom ---\n")
cat("Numerator df (k):", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df (n - k - 1):", df_den, "\n")
cat("\n--- Test Calculation ---\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (λ):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Critical F-value F(", df_num, ",", df_den, ",", alpha, "):", critical_F, "\n")
cat("Power (1 - sided, α = 0.05):", power, "\n")

# Return structured result
results_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)

cat("\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", results_json, "\n", sep = "")

plan.estimand: R-squared test against zero in linear regression with 4 model terms (intercept + 3 predictors)
plan.hypothesis: H0: R² = 0 vs H1: R² > 0 (noncentral F-test)
assumptions: Linear model specification correct
Predictors are fixed (not random)
Errors are normally distributed with constant variance
Multiple correlation ρ = 0.30 holds at population
No multicollinearity issues affecting F-test validity
One-sided test: H1 specifies R² > 0
scientific_notes: Power calculation for F-test of model significance uses noncentral F distribution
Noncentrality parameter λ = n × R² / (1 − R²) derived from effect size f² = R² / (1 − R²)
Numerator df = k = 3 (number of predictors)
Denominator df = n − k − 1 = 80 − 3 − 1 = 76
Critical value from central F(3, 76) at α = 0.05, then compare to noncentral F distribution

# Power calculation for R-squared test in linear regression
# H0: R^2 = 0 vs H1: R^2 > 0

# Parameters
n <- 80                          # Sample size
rho <- 0.30                      # Multiple correlation coefficient
k <- 3                           # Number of predictors (excluding intercept)
alpha <- 0.05                    # Significance level

# Degrees of freedom
df_num <- k                      # Numerator df = number of predictors
df_den <- n - k - 1             # Denominator df = n - k - 1

# Convert multiple correlation to R-squared
R2 <- rho^2

# Noncentrality parameter lambda for F-distribution
# lambda = n * R^2 / (1 - R^2)
lambda <- n * R2 / (1 - R2)

# Critical F-value from central F distribution at alpha = 0.05
critical_F <- qf(1 - alpha, df_num, df_den)

# Power = P(F > critical_F) under noncentral F distribution with noncentrality lambda
# Using pf with ncp parameter
power <- 1 - pf(critical_F, df_num, df_den, ncp = lambda)

# Summary output
cat("=== Linear Regression R-squared Power Calculation ===\n")
cat("Sample size (n):", n, "participants\n")
cat("Number of predictors (k):", k, "\n")
cat("Multiple correlation (ρ):", rho, "\n")
cat("R-squared:", R2, "\n")
cat("Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("\n--- Degrees of Freedom ---\n")
cat("Numerator df (k):", df_num, "\n")
cat("Denominator df (n - k - 1):", df_den, "\n")
cat("\n--- Test Calculation ---\n")
cat("Noncentrality parameter (λ):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Critical F-value F(", df_num, ",", df_den, ",", alpha, "):", critical_F, "\n")
cat("Power (1 - sided, α = 0.05):", power, "\n")

# Return structured result
results_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)

cat("\n")
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=", results_json, "\n", sep = "")

plan.estimand: Minimum total development sample size for survival prediction model meeting Riley criteria for model precision and calibration
plan.hypothesis: The developed prediction model will achieve adequate internal validity: (1) Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared ≥ 0.051 with shrinkage 0.90; (2) Nagelkerke R-squared apparent-adjusted difference ≤ 0.05; (3) Average outcome-risk prediction margin of error ≤ 0.05 on 95% CI at 2-year horizon
assumptions: Riley criteria framework for survival prediction model development
pmsampsize 1.1.3 package default implementation
Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared 0.051 represents prior or preliminary evidence of model discrimination
Event rate 0.065 per person-year applies uniformly across follow-up
Mean follow-up of 2.07 years reflects anticipated development cohort duration
Prediction horizon of 2 years aligns with clinical utility target
Shrinkage factor 0.90 reflects expected overfitting correction via validation/regularization
Nagelkerke scale R-squared used for apparent-adjusted discrimination difference
Average outcome-risk precision calculated at prediction horizon with 95% confidence interval
Sample size meets all three Riley criteria simultaneously (discrimination, calibration, precision)
scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2020, 2021) framework uses multidimensional criteria: (1) discrimination/R-squared shrinkage, (2) calibration slope shrinkage, (3) prediction precision (confidence interval width on absolute risk scale)
pmsampsize implements criterion-specific sample size minima; reported N is maximum across all three criteria
Cox-Snell R-squared in survival context differs from logistic R-squared; Nagelkerke rescaling used for harmonized comparison across outcome types
Event count (not just participants) influences precision criterion; total events N_events = N × event_rate × mean_follow_up for development cohort
Prediction margin of error 0.05 on 95% CI implies ±0.05 absolute risk; this constrains required event count for adequate precision at horizon
Shrinkage 0.90 assumes 10% overfitting; conservative but realistic for 30-predictor model without regularization
Verification will compute achieved prediction CI width at returned sample size and preceding admissible design

# Install and load pmsampsize if needed
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org/")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Verify package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Riley criteria for survival prediction model
# Inputs:
# type = "survival" for time-to-event prediction
# p = number of candidate predictor parameters
# r2 = adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (preliminary model performance)
# eventrate = overall event rate per person-year
# meanfup = mean follow-up duration in years
# horizon = prediction time horizon in years
# shrinkage = shrinkage factor (1 = no shrinkage, <1 = expect overfitting)
# alpha = significance level (default 0.05)
# target_moe = maximum absolute margin of error on outcome-risk scale (95% CI)

samplesize_survival <- pmsampsize(
  type = "survival",
  p = 30,                    # candidate predictor parameters
  r2 = 0.051,                # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  eventrate = 0.065,         # event rate per person-year
  meanfup = 2.07,            # mean follow-up in years
  horizon = 2,               # prediction horizon in years
  shrinkage = 0.90,          # shrinkage factor
  alpha = 0.05,              # significance level (two-tailed, default)
  target_moe = 0.05          # maximum absolute margin of error (95% CI)
)

# Display full output object
print(samplesize_survival)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size
min_n_participants <- min_n[which.max(min_n)]

# Also show component calculations
print("\n=== Component Sample Sizes by Criterion ===")
print(min_n)

# Display detailed results table
print("\n=== Detailed Results ===")
print(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation)

# Extract final minimum for reporting
final_n <- as.numeric(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size[
  which.max(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size)
])

# Expected event count at this sample size
expected_events <- final_n * 0.065 * 2.07

cat("\n=== Summary for Reporting ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (participants_total):", final_n, "\n")
cat("Expected total events:", round(expected_events, 2), "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", 0.90, "\n")
cat("Baseline Cox-Snell R-squared:", 0.051, "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     A list including a matrix of calculated sample size requirements
     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2

# Run the Riley criteria calculation one more time to capture results cleanly
samplesize_result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "s",

  parameters = 30,
  rate = 0.065,
  timepoint = 2,
  meanfup = 2.07,

n_total <- samplesize_result$sample_size
n_events <- samplesize_result$events
person_years <- samplesize_result$tot_per_yrs_final
shrinkage_final <- samplesize_result$final_shrinkage
cox_snell_rs <- samplesize_result$r2a
nagelkerke_rs <- samplesize_result$nag_r2
epp <- samplesize_result$EPP
ci_lower <- samplesize_result$int_lci
ci_upper <- samplesize_result$int_uci
risk_estimate <- samplesize_result$int_cuminc
event_rate <- samplesize_result$rate
timepoint <- samplesize_result$timepoint
meanfup <- samplesize_result$meanfup

# Verify precision criterion: ±0.05 margin of error at 95% CI
# Margin of error = (CI_upper - CI_lower) / 2
moe_achieved <- (ci_upper - ci_lower) / 2
moe_target <- 0.05

cat("=== VERIFICATION: Prediction Precision Criterion ===\n")
cat("Sample size N:", n_total, "participants\n")
cat("Expected events:", n_events, "\n")
cat("Expected person-time:", person_years, "person-years\n\n")

cat("95% Confidence Interval for overall 2-year risk:\n")
cat("  Lower bound: ", ci_lower, "\n")
cat("  Upper bound: ", ci_upper, "\n")
cat("  Point estimate: ", risk_estimate, "\n")
cat("  CI width: ", ci_upper - ci_lower, "\n")
cat("  Margin of error (half-width): ", moe_achieved, "\n\n")

cat("Criterion requirement: Margin of error ≤ 0.05\n")
cat("Achieved margin of error: ", moe_achieved, "\n")
cat("Status: ", if(moe_achieved <= moe_target) "✓ MEETS criterion" else "✗ FAILS criterion", "\n\n")

# Check preceding admissible design (test with N = 5142)
cat("=== VERIFICATION: Preceding Design (N - 1 = 5142) ===\n")
n_minus_one <- n_total - 1
person_years_minus_one <- n_minus_one * meanfup
events_minus_one <- person_years_minus_one * event_rate

cat("Sample size N:", n_minus_one, "participants\n")
cat("Expected person-time:", round(person_years_minus_one, 2), "person-years\n")
cat("Expected events:", round(events_minus_one, 2), "\n\n")

# For survival outcome, precision for overall risk follows binomial-like logic
# At timepoint, the standard error of cumulative incidence is approximately:
# SE ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/events) where p is the probability of event by timepoint
# 95% CI half-width ≈ 1.96 * SE

p_event_2yr <- risk_estimate
se_n_5142 <- sqrt(p_event_2yr * (1 - p_event_2yr) / round(events_minus_one, 0))
moe_5142 <- 1.96 * se_n_5142

plan.estimand: Minimum total development sample size for survival prediction model meeting Riley criteria for model precision and calibration
plan.hypothesis: The developed prediction model will achieve adequate internal validity: (1) Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared ≥ 0.051 with shrinkage 0.90; (2) Nagelkerke R-squared apparent-adjusted difference ≤ 0.05; (3) Average outcome-risk prediction margin of error ≤ 0.05 on 95% CI at 2-year horizon
assumptions: Riley criteria framework for survival prediction model development
pmsampsize 1.1.3 package default implementation
Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared 0.051 represents prior or preliminary evidence of model discrimination
Event rate 0.065 per person-year applies uniformly across follow-up
Mean follow-up of 2.07 years reflects anticipated development cohort duration
Prediction horizon of 2 years aligns with clinical utility target
Shrinkage factor 0.90 reflects expected overfitting correction via validation/regularization
Nagelkerke scale R-squared used for apparent-adjusted discrimination difference
Average outcome-risk precision calculated at prediction horizon with 95% confidence interval
Sample size meets all three Riley criteria simultaneously (discrimination, calibration, precision)
scientific_notes: Riley et al. (2020, 2021) framework uses multidimensional criteria: (1) discrimination/R-squared shrinkage, (2) calibration slope shrinkage, (3) prediction precision (confidence interval width on absolute risk scale)
pmsampsize implements criterion-specific sample size minima; reported N is maximum across all three criteria
Cox-Snell R-squared in survival context differs from logistic R-squared; Nagelkerke rescaling used for harmonized comparison across outcome types
Event count (not just participants) influences precision criterion; total events N_events = N × event_rate × mean_follow_up for development cohort
Prediction margin of error 0.05 on 95% CI implies ±0.05 absolute risk; this constrains required event count for adequate precision at horizon
Shrinkage 0.90 assumes 10% overfitting; conservative but realistic for 30-predictor model without regularization
Verification will compute achieved prediction CI width at returned sample size and preceding admissible design

# Install and load pmsampsize if needed
if (!requireNamespace("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org/")
}
library(pmsampsize)

# Verify package version
packageVersion("pmsampsize")

# Riley criteria for survival prediction model
# Inputs:
# type = "survival" for time-to-event prediction
# p = number of candidate predictor parameters
# r2 = adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (preliminary model performance)
# eventrate = overall event rate per person-year
# meanfup = mean follow-up duration in years
# horizon = prediction time horizon in years
# shrinkage = shrinkage factor (1 = no shrinkage, <1 = expect overfitting)
# alpha = significance level (default 0.05)
# target_moe = maximum absolute margin of error on outcome-risk scale (95% CI)

samplesize_survival <- pmsampsize(
  type = "survival",
  p = 30,                    # candidate predictor parameters
  r2 = 0.051,                # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  eventrate = 0.065,         # event rate per person-year
  meanfup = 2.07,            # mean follow-up in years
  horizon = 2,               # prediction horizon in years
  shrinkage = 0.90,          # shrinkage factor
  alpha = 0.05,              # significance level (two-tailed, default)
  target_moe = 0.05          # maximum absolute margin of error (95% CI)
)

# Display full output object
print(samplesize_survival)

# Extract the minimum sample size
min_n <- samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size
min_n_participants <- min_n[which.max(min_n)]

# Also show component calculations
print("\n=== Component Sample Sizes by Criterion ===")
print(min_n)

# Display detailed results table
print("\n=== Detailed Results ===")
print(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation)

# Extract final minimum for reporting
final_n <- as.numeric(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size[
  which.max(samplesize_survival$sample_size_calculation$Minimum_sample_size)
])

# Expected event count at this sample size
expected_events <- final_n * 0.065 * 2.07

cat("\n=== Summary for Reporting ===\n")
cat("Minimum total sample size (participants_total):", final_n, "\n")
cat("Expected total events:", round(expected_events, 2), "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", 0.90, "\n")
cat("Baseline Cox-Snell R-squared:", 0.051, "\n")
